name: Mexico
summary_text: Mexico has no national administrative procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures had enacted none at all. Only seven states extend recognition to children.  In 2022 the Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where no procedure exists, trans people are left carrying identity documents that contradict their lived gender, and that mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. Recognition therefore depends on the state a person is in.  Tabasco, documented jointly by Human Rights Watch and the Community Center for Inclusion on 6 March 2024, had no legal gender-recognition procedure. There, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions.  The protective machinery is weak. More than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and the Tabasco material includes the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa.

name: Mayotte
summary_text: Mayotte stands under France's national framework. Identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France, and the French prison rules bind the island's places of deprivation of liberty as French establishments.  Nothing in that framework criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been available on the island since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975, and it is one of the few jurisdictions in Africa and the Muslim-majority world where such marriages can be performed. The National Assembly's vote simplifying legal gender change for trans people likewise extends to the department.  Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Trans women are therefore typically held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; anatomy does not decide where a person is placed.  The national detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. The finding rests on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on site inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed, at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. Because these are French establishments, the same standards and the same documented failures govern any facility holding a trans person on Mayotte.  Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge on the island. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023 only after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the law on paper is not the whole of what a couple faces.  Legal representation is thinly available locally. A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while listing a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, working in persons and family law, as available.

sources.title: Penal Code of 1791 and Penal Code of 1810
sources.documents: Decriminalisation of same-sex sexual activity in private in France; retained policy followed in French colonies. Establishes baseline legal status applicable to Mayotte as French territory.
